newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka to pay for some ammunition from $63 mln deal.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka to pay for some ammunition from $63 mln deal.

text.p: The Sri Lankan navy will partly pay the Chinese supplier involved in a controversial $63 million arms deal that will leave the country with a huge stockpile of ammunition, a newspaper reported on Sunday.
Naval chief Vice-Admiral Cecil Tissera told the Sunday Leader newspaper in an interview that the navy, which is investigating the deal, would only pay for what it used.
The remaining ammunition would be kept in a bonded warehouse for the Chinese company in Sri Lanka, he said.

Newspaper reports said earlier this month that $63 million worth of ammunition, mostly 35 millimetre and 25 millimetre high-explosive shells for use by the navy's ageing Chinese-built gunboats, had been sitting in Colombo port since mid-January.
They said it would take 30 years to use the quantity bought by the navy, much longer than the ammunition's shelf-life.
The ammunition deal was struck in 1995 during the tenure of Tissera's predecessor. Tissera took over as naval chief earlier this year.
"We will pay only for the ammunition used by us. The Chinese company is at liberty to sell the balance to any country or dispose of them of in any other way," Tissera told the newspaper.
He said investigations into the deal were over and that he would soon submit a report to the defence ministry.
"We are inquiring why such a large order was placed, how it happened and why the ammunition was sent even when the order was cancelled," he added.
"It could be that the company believed there would be no problem as it was establishing a bonded warehouse here."

Six Shanghai-class gunboats spearhead the navy's fleet in its battle against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels, who are waging a war, now in its 14th year, for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east.
Tissera said the Chinese company had sent 150,000 rounds of 25 mm and 35 mm shells, whereas the annual consumption of these shells by the Sri Lankan navy was only 3,000.
